surfaces.part: mug and beer in the window

answer.evidence: The main body is the 12px-wide cabinet at rows 10-30. Its rows 11-14 form a light band (L=208-242), with a darker front-edge line at row 15. The dark window interior at rows 16-23 follows as eave shadow, and below it the front face has a window, a mug and a grille, down to row 30. That gives a top band of about 4 rows over a front face of about 15 rows, similar to the green cabinet reference. The narrower upper tower (rows 1-9) has only a light gradient at rows 2-5 above a blue label and no clear front-edge line, so it is a weaker top. The evidence for a top surface is moderate, since the band could also be read as a front-facing cornice.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small white and grey body with a blue jug on top, about one tile wide and two tall. Measured density is fine: 11 visible tones per tile against 9 for the hedge, and 0% near-flat coverage. The problem is structure. Every material (jug, body, base) has only about 3 lightness steps, where the cheese stall and well use 5-6. The dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the shape is wrapped in a uniform black/grey outline rather than a darker tone of the neighbouring material. This is the 'sticker' look. Only the lamp reference is also neutral, and that is a metal pole. The stall and well references use tinted outlines (1% and 33% neutral). The surfaces are smooth with little grain, tile highlights or per-part shading, so the piece looks thinner and flatter than the stall and well beside it. When in doubt, fail.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small water-cooler-style server with a pale jug on top, a white body, a tap and a mug. The problem is the outline and the shading. 100% of its dark edge pixels are neutral, so it reads as a uniform black/grey sticker line around every shape. The references with rich material shading (hedge 0%, cheese stall 1%, well 33%) use tinted, material-toned darks instead. The body and jug show only about 3 lightness steps each (white, light grey, dark) with little grain, against 5-6 steps per material in Beodeul. Next to the stall and well it looks thinner and more sticker-like, so it fails on outline craft and shading depth.

surfaces.part: main body front with window and contents

answer.evidence: The silhouette is a narrower upper block (rows 1-9, width 8) on a wider body (rows 10-30, width 12). Row 10 is a full dark outline that separates them. The upper block has a vertical light gradient (rows 2-5) and a blue label (rows 6-9), which read as a face-on front, not a horizontal surface. The body starts with a light plate (rows 11-14) bounded by a dark row 15, but it repeats in the bottom plate (rows 24-29) with the same light/dark pattern, so it is a front-facing panel, not a top with an edge line and eave shadow. No ellipse, roof, or visible contents from above. Below it the front shows a window with a yellow glass (rows 16-23) and the bottom panel. Nothing shows a receding top, so the drawing is a flat front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small, narrow dispenser, about one tile wide, with a jug on top. The 100% near-neutral dark edge share shows a neutral black/grey outline around the whole silhouette, the 'sticker' look. Beodeul pieces like the stall (1%), hedge (0%) and well (33%) use tinted, material-toned edges instead. The body is mostly white/grey with a blue jug, and each material has only about 3 lightness steps (highlight, mid, dark), compared with 5-6 on the references. Grain, speckle and per-material ramps are minimal. It is clean and not flat-filled, but it looks thinner and more outlined than the references, so it does not match the Beodeul standard.

answer.evidence: The main body (rows 10-30, width 12) starts with a dark outline at row 10. Rows 11-14 form a light band (L about 208-242), and row 15 is a darker 1-row line (L=91) that reads as its front edge. Below that is a front face of about 15 rows (rows 16-30): a recessed window with a mug and a lower grille. The narrower upper head (rows 1-9, width 8) repeats the pattern with a light band at rows 2-5 and a dark line at row 6 above the blue label. The band is only moderately convincing as a top surface, since it could also be a front-facing header strip, but it has an edge line and sits above a darker face, so I read it as a top.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small, roughly one-tile-wide, two-tile-tall water-cooler-style server with a pale body, a blue jug on top and a small tap. Its ramps are shallow: the white/grey body reads as about 3 steps, and the jug and tap as 2-3 each. The references use 5-6 steps per material. The measured dark edge pixels are 100% near-neutral, so the outline is a uniform black/grey line with no tint from the adjacent material. That is the sticker look, in contrast with the tinted outlines on the stall (1% neutral), the hedge (0%) and the well (33%). Tone count is 11 per tile with 0% near-flat coverage. That is comparable to the hedge (9) but below the stall (17) and well (20), which are the closest references for a furnished prop. By eye, the body has little grain or per-surface texture, and it looks flatter and thinner than the stall counter or well masonry. The lamp-crook reference also has a neutral outline, but it is a thin iron pole where that is natural. Here a neutral outline around a multi-material prop reads as shallow. Overall it is cleanly drawn but not at the Beodeul bar.
